c.title: Households with broadband access in three countries, 2004-2024

x: The line graph compares the proportion of homes with a broadband connection in Canada, Brazil and India over a 20-year period starting in 2004.
Overall, broadband access rose in all three countries. Canada had the highest level of access throughout, while India, which started from almost zero, saw the fastest growth in the final decade.

In 2004, just over a third of Canadian households (35%) had broadband, compared with only 8% in Brazil and a mere 1% in India. Over the next ten years, the Canadian figure more than doubled to 78%, and Brazil's rose to 41%. India, by contrast, made little progress, reaching just 9% by 2014.

From 2014 onwards, growth in Canada slowed as it neared full coverage, with the proportion edging up to 92% by 2024. Brazil continued to climb at a steady pace, ending the period at 74%. The most dramatic change occurred in India, where access tripled to 28% in 2019 and then nearly doubled again to 55% in 2024, although this was still well below the other two countries.
notes: Intro te 'shows' er bodole 'compares', 'percentage of households' er bodole 'proportion of homes', '2004 and 2024' er bodole 'a 20-year period starting in 2004'.
Overview e kono number nai, shudhu duita boro kotha: shobai bereche, Canada top, India fastest growth.
Body bhag kora time diye: 2004-2014 ar 2014-2024. Eta line graph er jonno shohoj grouping.
Number er sathe meaning: 'just over a third (35%)', 'more than doubled', 'tripled'. Shudhu number list na.

The pie charts show how energy consumption in homes in one country was divided among five uses in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, heating was the largest single use of household energy in both years, although its share fell considerably. The most striking change was the rise of appliances, which had become the second biggest category by 2020.

In 1990, heating alone accounted for just over half of all domestic energy use (52%). Water heating came a distant second at 20%, while lighting, appliances and cooking each made up roughly a tenth of the total, at 11%, 9% and 8% respectively.

Thirty years later, the share used for heating had dropped to 38%, and lighting's portion had fallen by almost half to 6%. Water heating also declined slightly, to 18%. In contrast, the proportion consumed by appliances tripled from 9% to 27%, overtaking water heating. Cooking was the only other category to grow, rising modestly from 8% to 11%.

The bar chart compares the average amount of water used by one person each day in five cities in 2010 and 2020.
Overall, Perth residents used by far the most water in both years, although consumption there and in Oslo went down. In the other three cities, daily use per person increased over the decade.

In 2010, the average person in Perth used 260 litres a day, almost three times the figure for Lima (95 litres), the lowest of the five. Oslo was a distant second at 180 litres, while Cairo and Dhaka recorded 140 and 110 litres respectively.

Overall, the country moved sharply away from coal over the period. Coal went from being the largest source to the smallest, while gas and renewables both expanded, with renewables showing the most rapid growth in the final decade.

Overall, the share of older people has risen in all three countries and is expected to keep rising. The most striking change is in Japan, which had the youngest population of the three in 1960 but is predicted to have by far the oldest by 2040.

In 1960, only 6% of Japanese people were 65 or over, compared with 9% in the USA and 12% in Sweden. Sweden's figure rose to 16% by 1980 and 17% by 2000, while the American proportion grew only slightly, to 12% in 2000.

Japan's figure increased gradually until 1980 (9%) and then much faster, matching Sweden at 17% in 2000 and reaching 29% in 2020. It is projected to rise further to 35% in 2040, which would be around 12 or 13 percentage points above the other two countries. Over the same period, the proportions in Sweden and the USA are expected to climb more slowly, to 23% and 22% respectively, almost closing the gap between them.

Number bachai: men 58, 49, 36, 24; women 44, 42, 38/33, 22. Shob 12 ta na.
The bar chart compares the percentages of men and women in one country who exercised regularly in 2022, broken down into six age groups.

Overall, participation in regular exercise fell steadily with age for both sexes. Men were noticeably more active than women in the two youngest groups, but this pattern was reversed in middle age, and the figures for the two sexes were broadly similar from the age of 35 onwards.

Among 16 to 24-year-olds, 58% of men exercised regularly, compared with 46% of women, the widest gap on the chart. For men, the figure dropped with each older age group, to 49% for those aged 25 to 34 and 36% for the 45 to 54 group, before falling to just 24% among the over-65s.

The decline for women was much more gradual. Their rate stood at 44% in the 25 to 34 group and 42% in the 35 to 44 group, slightly above the male figure of 41%. Women remained marginally ahead in the next two groups as well (38% and 33%, against 36% and 30% for men). In the oldest group, however, men were again slightly more active, at 24% compared with 22%.

'the widest gap on the chart' diye important feature highlight kora.

x: Food

x: The bar chart shows how much an average family in one country spent each week on food, housing, transport and entertainment in 1980, 2000 and 2020.

Overall, spending on all four categories increased over the forty years. Housing was the largest expense in every year and also saw the biggest rise, while entertainment, though still the smallest item, grew at the fastest rate.

In 1980, a typical family spent $60 a week on housing and $45 on food, compared with only $20 on transport and $10 on entertainment. By 2000, housing costs had risen to $95, and by 2020 they had reached $150, two and a half times the 1980 figure. Food spending, in contrast, grew relatively slowly, from $45 to $55 and then to $62.

Transport costs almost doubled between 1980 and 2000, from $20 to $38, but rose only modestly after that, to $45 in 2020. Entertainment showed the most dramatic change: weekly spending more than doubled to $22 in 2000 and then nearly doubled again to $41, so that by 2020 it was not far behind transport.

x: The bar chart compares the main reasons undergraduate and postgraduate students at a university gave for choosing their course.

Overall, career prospects were the most common reason in both groups, followed by personal interest. The biggest difference between the two groups concerned family advice, which mattered far more to undergraduates than to postgraduates.

The pie charts compare how the average household in one country divided its spending between six categories in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the pattern of spending changed considerably over the 30 years. Food, the largest item in 1990, lost its top position to housing, while the shares spent on transport, healthcare and education all increased.

In 1990, food took up 38% of household budgets, well ahead of housing at 22%. By 2020, these positions had been reversed: housing accounted for a third of spending (33%), while the proportion going on food had fallen to 21%, little more than half its earlier level. Taken together, these two essentials made up 60% of spending in 1990 but 54% in 2020.

The three service categories each took a larger share by the end of the period. Transport rose from 10% to 15% and education from 9% to 12%, while healthcare almost doubled, from 6% to 11%. The only other category to shrink was miscellaneous spending, labelled 'other', which dropped from 15% to just 8%.

Overall, there was a clear shift away from the car towards other forms of transport. The car was the most common way of getting to the university in 2005, but by 2025 the bus had taken first place and cycling had become far more popular.
In 2005, 41% of students travelled by car, considerably more than the 26% who took the bus. Walking was the third most common method (16%), followed by cycling (9%) and the train (8%).

The table gives the number of international students in five countries in 2010, 2015 and 2020, in thousands.

Overall, the USA hosted by far the most international students in all three years. Every country except the USA saw continuous growth, and the most rapid expansion was in Canada, where student numbers more than tripled.

The USA's total rose sharply from 690,000 in 2010 to 970,000 in 2015, before falling slightly to 910,000 in 2020. Even after this decline, it remained well ahead of the UK, the second most popular destination, which had 550,000 international students in 2020. The UK's figure had changed little between 2010 and 2015 (410,000 and 430,000) before rising more noticeably in the following five years.

Among the three smaller destinations, Australia doubled its intake, from 230,000 to 460,000. c.title: The production of black tea
steps: Packed in boxes or tea bags

x: The diagram illustrates how black tea is produced, from the moment the leaves are picked to the point where the packed tea reaches shops.

Overall, the process consists of eight stages and is largely mechanical once the leaves have been harvested. Only the first step is carried out by hand, while the middle stages change the leaves physically and chemically before the tea is graded, packed and sent out.

The process begins when fresh tea leaves are picked by hand. They are then spread out and left to wither for 12 to 18 hours. Next, the withered leaves are rolled by machine and left to ferment, a stage known as oxidation. After fermentation, the leaves are dried with hot air, which completes the main processing stage.

Once the leaves are dry, they are sorted and graded according to their size. The graded tea is then packed, either loose in boxes or in tea bags, and in the final stage it is transported to shops, where it is sold to consumers.
notes: Introduction prompt copy kore na, 'stages in the production' ke 'how black tea is produced' bananu hoyeche.

Sequencers vary kore: begins when, then, Next, After fermentation, Once the leaves are dry, in the final stage.

The diagram below shows the life cycle of a frog.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: The life cycle of a frog

x: The diagram shows the life cycle of a frog, from the laying of eggs to the stage at which a fully grown frog is ready to reproduce.

Overall, there are eight main stages in this natural cycle, which takes roughly 12 to 16 weeks to complete. The most striking feature is the gradual change from a tadpole that lives in water and breathes through gills into an adult that can survive on land.

The cycle starts when an adult frog lays a mass of eggs, known as spawn, in water. After about ten days, tadpoles hatch from these eggs, and at this early point they breathe through gills. Their back legs then start to grow at around six to nine weeks, and by roughly the twelfth week the front legs have also appeared.

In the following stage, the tail shrinks and the young animal develops lungs, which allows it to breathe air. It is now a froglet and leaves the water. Finally, it grows into an adult frog at 12 to 16 weeks, and the cycle begins again when this frog lays its own eggs.
notes: Natural process bole active verbs: hatch, grow, appear, shrinks, develops. Passive force kora hoy nai.

The biggest changes have taken place north of Main Road. pages.h: Practice 1: line graph with four lines

blocks.x: Char ta line thakle protiti line alada describe korle answer lomba ar boring hoy. Group koro: car ar bus (falling after peak / falling), bicycle ar metro (rising at the end).

The graph below shows the percentage of commuters in one city who used four different modes of transport to travel to work between 1990 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Percentage of commuters using four modes of transport in one city, 1990-2020

x: The line graph illustrates how commuters in one city travelled to work between 1990 and 2020, comparing the share who used cars, buses, bicycles and the metro.

Overall, the car remained the most common way to commute throughout the period, although its popularity peaked in 2005 and then declined. The metro showed the strongest growth, while bus use fell steadily and cycling recovered after an early drop.

In 1990, 42% of commuters drove to work, and this figure rose to a high of 52% in 2005. After that, it fell back gradually to 40% in 2020. The bus was the second most popular option at the start, used by 35% of workers, but its share decreased in every period, ending at just 21%.

The metro carried only 8% of commuters in 1990 and 1995, yet its share climbed to 22% by 2020, overtaking the bus in the final year. Cycling followed a different pattern: it dropped from 15% to a low of 9% in 2005, then rose again to 17%, although it was still the least common choice in 2020.
notes: Overview e 4 ta line er main movement eksathe: car top, metro fastest growth, bus falling, cycling recovery.
Crossing point (metro overtaking the bus in 2020) dhora hoyeche, jeta key feature.
Peak ar low exact year shoho: 52% in 2005, 9% in 2005.
Verb variety: rose, fell back, decreased, climbed, dropped, overtaking.
Body 1 e falling/peaking line, body 2 e rising line, tai grouping logical.

blocks.x: Ekta line 0 theke shuru hole 'made no contribution', 'from nothing', 'was not used at all' er moto phrase lage. Ar duita line jekhane cross kore, seta overview ba body te mention koro.

The graph below shows the amount of electricity generated from gas, coal and solar power in one country between 2000 and 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Electricity generated from three sources in one country, 2000-2024

x: The line graph compares the amount of electricity a country produced from gas, coal and solar power between 2000 and 2024, measured in terawatt hours (TWh).

Overall, gas was by far the largest source of electricity throughout the period, and its output more than doubled. Solar power grew from nothing to become the second largest source, whereas coal declined after 2012.

Gas-fired generation stood at 20 TWh in 2000 and increased steadily, reaching a peak of 50 TWh in 2020 before dipping slightly to 48 TWh in 2024. Coal, by contrast, produced 12 TWh at the start and rose only modestly to 15 TWh in 2008, where it stayed until 2012. From then on, it fell in each period, ending at 8 TWh.

Solar power made no contribution in 2000 and 2004, and its output remained very small, at 1 to 2 TWh, until 2012. After this point, however, it rose sharply, to 12 TWh in 2020 and 18 TWh in 2024. As a result, solar had overtaken coal by 2020 and generated more than twice as much electricity as coal by the end of the period.
notes: Unit (TWh) introduction e ekbar full form e, tarpor short form e.
'more than doubled' ar 'more than twice as much' duitai math e thik (20 to 48, 18 vs 8).
'had overtaken coal by 2020' te past perfect, grammar range dekhay.
Stable phase ('where it stayed until 2012') miss kora hoy nai.
Contrast linkers natural jaygay: by contrast, however, whereas.

pages.h: Practice 3: bar chart by age group

blocks.x: Bar chart e category (age group) gulo x axis e. Ekhane main story holo duita activity opposite direction e jay. Overview e eta dhorte parlei half kaj shesh.

The chart below shows the average number of hours per week that people in four age groups spent on four leisure activities.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Average hours per week spent on four leisure activities, by age group

x: The bar chart shows the average number of hours people in four age groups spent each week on social media, television, sport and reading.

Overall, younger people devoted most of their free time to social media, while older people spent the most time watching TV. Time spent on sport fell with age, whereas reading became more popular in older groups.

The 15-24 age group spent 18 hours a week on social media, the highest figure in the chart. This dropped sharply with age, to 11 hours among 25 to 44-year-olds, 6 hours for those aged 45-64 and just 3 hours for people over 65. Television showed the reverse pattern, rising from 7 hours for the youngest group to 20 hours for the oldest, which made it the top activity for both of the older groups.

The other two activities took up much less time. Young people played sport for 6 hours a week, but this halved to 3 hours in the 45-64 group and fell to only 2 hours among the over-65s. Reading moved in the opposite direction, increasing from 3 hours to 8 hours across the four age groups.
notes: Overview e 4 ta activity er direction: social media down, TV up, sport down, reading up.
Biggest figure (18 hours) ar biggest value overall (20 hours) dui ta clearly highlighted.
Age group er bhasha vary kora: the 15-24 age group, 25 to 44-year-olds, those aged 45-64, the over-65s.
'halved' accurate (6 to 3), ar 'reverse pattern', 'opposite direction' comparison toiri kore.
Body split: boro activity (social media, TV) ar choto activity (sport, reading).

blocks.x: Duita pie mane duita time point er share. Biggest slice change hole (food theke housing) eta main feature. Percentage change bolar shomoy 'percentage points' sathik vabe use koro.

The pie charts below show how the average household in one country spent its money in 2000 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Average household spending in one country, 2000 and 2020

x: The pie charts compare how the average household in one country divided its spending between six categories in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, food was the biggest expense in 2000, but by 2020 housing had taken its place. The shares spent on housing, transport, education and health all grew, while food and other items took up a smaller part of the budget.

In 2000, food accounted for 38% of household spending, considerably more than housing, which made up 22%. Twenty years later, the proportion spent on food had fallen to 26%, while housing costs had risen to 30%, making housing the largest single category. The gap between these two categories therefore reversed, from 16 points in favour of food to 4 points in favour of housing.

The remaining categories were much smaller. Transport rose from 12% to 15% of spending, and the share devoted to education went up from 8% to 11%. Health showed a similar increase of three percentage points, from 6% to 9%. In contrast, the 'other' category dropped from 14% to 9%, so in 2020 it was equal to health and slightly below education.
notes: Main feature (food ar housing er jayga bodol) overview ar body 1 duitai te ache.
'percentage points' sathik use: 6% to 9% holo three percentage points.
Share er bhasha vary: accounted for, made up, the proportion spent on, the share devoted to.
Choto category gulo group kore ekta paragraph e, tai answer lomba hoy nai.
2020 er comparison (other = health, below education) dekhay je writer data ta analyse korche.

blocks.x: Table e onek number, tai selection skill test hoy. Protiti row er start ar end, plus kono row er direction alada hole seta. Shob middle number dite hobe na.

The table below shows the number of students enrolled in four courses at one university in 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: Number of students enrolled in four courses at one university

x: The table gives the number of students enrolled in four university courses in 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Overall, Computer Science grew the fastest and became the most popular course, while English Literature was the only subject to lose students steadily. Business and Engineering changed relatively little.

Computer Science had 820 students in 2010, but this figure rose to 1,340 in 2015 and to 2,150 in 2020, more than two and a half times the original number. As a result, it overtook Business, which had been the largest course at the start with 1,500 students. Business enrolment rose slightly to 1,620 in 2015 before dipping to 1,580 in 2020, which left it 570 students behind Computer Science.

Engineering attracted 960 students in 2010 and saw modest growth, to 1,010 and then 1,180. English Literature, on the other hand, declined sharply. Its enrolment fell from 640 to 470 and then to 310, so by 2020 it had less than half the number of students it had a decade earlier.
notes: Overview e fastest growth, only decline ar stable courses: table er 3 ta pattern.
Math accurate: 2,150 is more than 2.5 times 820; 310 is less than half of 640.
Ranking change ('overtook Business') ekta key feature, seta dhora hoyeche.
Number format thik: 1,340, 2,150 (comma diye), kono lakh ba crore nai.
Past perfect 'which had been the largest course' diye complex sentence.

blocks.x: Mixed task e duita chart er relation thakte pare, na o thakte pare. Introduction ar overview e duitai mention koro. Time beshi lage, tai prottekta chart theke 3 to 4 ta key point e jothesto.

The line graph below shows the number of adults and children who visited the City Science Museum between 2016 and 2024. The pie chart shows the main reasons visitors gave for their visit in 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

charts.title: Visitors to the City Science Museum, 2016-2024

x: The line graph shows the number of adults and children who visited the City Science Museum between 2016 and 2024, and the pie chart shows visitors' main reasons for coming in 2024.

Overall, visitor numbers for both groups rose apart from a sharp fall in 2020, and both had reached their highest levels by 2024. In that year, school trips and family days out were the most common reasons for a visit.

In 2016, the museum received 120,000 adult visitors and 80,000 children. These figures grew to 135,000 and 95,000 respectively in 2018. In 2020, however, attendance collapsed to only 40,000 adults and 25,000 children. Numbers then rebounded strongly, reaching 110,000 and 90,000 in 2022 and rising further to 150,000 adults and 130,000 children in 2024. The gap between the two groups narrowed over the period, from 40,000 to 20,000.

According to the 2024 survey, 34% of visitors came as part of a school trip and 28% for a family day out. Special exhibitions attracted 22%, while tourism accounted for 10% and other reasons for just 6%.
notes: Introduction e duita chart, overview e duita chart er main point.
'thousands' unit theke full number (120,000) e convert kora, reader er jonno clear.
'respectively' sathik use: duita list same order e.
Gap narrowing (40,000 to 20,000) ekta smart comparison jeta chart e direct lekha nai kintu calculate kora jay.
Pie paragraph choto kintu shob slice accurately covered.

blocks.x: 9 stage er linear process. Split point: pulp clean howa porjonto (stage 1 to 5) ar sheet banano (stage 6 to 9). Passive present simple shuru theke shesh.

The diagram below shows how recycled paper is made.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: How recycled paper is made
steps: Mixed with water to form pulp
Pressed between rollers to remove water
Cut into sheets and delivered to shops

x: The diagram illustrates the stages involved in turning used paper into new paper products that can be sold in shops.

Overall, there are nine stages in this linear process, beginning with the collection of waste paper and ending with the delivery of new paper to shops. The first half focuses on turning old paper into clean pulp, while the second half reforms this pulp into sheets.

First, used paper is collected and then sorted according to type and grade. It is then mixed with water to produce pulp. At the next stage, the ink is removed from the pulp in a process called de-inking, after which the pulp is cleaned further and whitened. By this point, the old paper has been fully converted into clean, white pulp.

Once the pulp is clean, it is pressed between rollers in order to remove the water. The pressed material then passes over heated rollers, which dry it. The dry paper is wound into large reels, and these are later cut into sheets. In the final step, the finished paper is delivered to shops.
notes: Overview e stage count, linear type, start ar end, plus duita phase.
Passive range: is collected, is removed, are later cut, is delivered.
Sequencing vary: First, then, At the next stage, after which, Once, In the final step.
Technical term (de-inking) diagram theke niye explain kora hoyeche, notun info add kora hoy nai.
Ekta active sentence ('passes over heated rollers') variety ane, meaning thik rekhe.

blocks.x: 1980 ar 2020, duitai past, tai past simple passive. Main story: farming ar fishing village theke tourist resort. Body split: road er north (inland) ar road er south (coast).

The maps below show a coastal village in 1980 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

c.title: A coastal village in 1980 and 2020

x: The maps show how a small coastal village changed between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the village was transformed from a farming and fishing community into a tourist resort. Most of the farmland, the fishing huts and part of the forest gave way to tourist facilities, although the coast road and the main residential area remained.

In 1980, a large area of farmland covered the north-west of the village. By 2020, the western half of this land had become a golf course, while holiday apartments had been built on the eastern half. The village houses to the east of this area were extended southwards, and the forest in the north-east was reduced in size, with a car park built on the cleared land.

Along the coast, south of the coast road, the fishing huts were demolished and replaced by a larger hotel, and a new restaurant was built to the east of it. The jetty that ran out towards the sea was also removed, and a marina was constructed in roughly the same position.
notes: Overview e character change (farming and fishing to tourism) ar ki same ache, duitai.
Past simple ar past perfect ('By 2020 ... had become') er sathik mix.
Change verbs vary: gave way to, had been built, were extended, was reduced in size, were demolished, was constructed.
Location phrase protiti item e: in the north-west, to the east of this area, south of the coast road.
Body split inland vs coast, map er geography follow kore.

x: Who should pay for higher education is a politically sensitive question, and some argue that students themselves ought to cover the entire cost of their degrees, since they are the ones who later earn higher salaries. I largely disagree with this view: although graduates do gain personally, society gains at least as much, so the cost should be shared.

It is true that a degree often brings private rewards. Graduates in most economies earn considerably more over their working lives than people who left education at eighteen, and they tend to have more secure jobs. From this perspective, asking taxpayers who never attended university to fund someone else's advantage seems unfair. A student who goes on to become a corporate lawyer, for instance, could reasonably be expected to repay at least part of what her training cost.

However, this argument ignores the wider returns that education brings. A country needs doctors, engineers and teachers, and if training for these professions became extremely expensive, many talented young people from low-income families would simply not apply. The result would be a smaller and less diverse pool of professionals, which would harm everyone who relies on public services. Educated citizens also pay more tax and are more likely to take part in civic life, so the state recovers much of its investment indirectly.

A fairer approach would be a shared model in which the government pays a large portion of tuition and graduates contribute through an income-linked loan once they earn above a certain threshold. This would protect access for poorer students while still recognising the personal benefit of a degree.

In conclusion, although graduates clearly benefit as individuals, I do not believe they should bear the full cost of their studies, because the gains from higher education are spread across the whole of society.

blocks.x: More and more people are working from home rather than in an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?

x: Since 2020, a growing number of employees have swapped the office for their kitchen table, and many companies now let staff work remotely for at least part of the week. Although this shift has some real drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater.

The main concern about remote work is its effect on relationships between colleagues. Much of what employees learn happens informally, by overhearing a conversation or asking a quick question at the next desk. When everyone is at home, these chances largely disappear, and new staff in particular may take longer to understand how their organisation works. Some people also find it hard to separate work from home life, especially if they live in small flats with no space for a desk.

These problems, however, are outweighed by the advantages. For many workers, the most obvious gain is time. A commuter in a congested city such as Dhaka can easily spend three hours a day travelling, and working from home returns that time for sleep, exercise or family. Employees also save money on transport and meals, which matters more as living costs rise. Employers benefit too: they can rent smaller offices and recruit talented people who live far from the city. What is more, fewer cars on the road during rush hour means less congestion and cleaner air for everyone.

Many of the drawbacks, in addition, can be reduced. Companies that bring teams together one or two days a week keep most of the social benefits of an office while still allowing staff to avoid daily travel.

In conclusion, although working from home can weaken team relationships, the time, money and environmental savings it brings make it a positive development, particularly when it is combined with regular face-to-face contact.

blocks.x: In many cities, young people are finding it increasingly difficult to afford a place to live. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?

x: In many large cities, young adults now spend such a high share of their income on rent that buying a home seems out of reach. This essay argues that the problem stems mainly from a shortage of new housing and from property being treated as an investment, and that both causes can be addressed by government action.

The most obvious cause is that housing supply has not kept pace with demand. As jobs become concentrated in a few major cities, people move there in large numbers, but planning rules and slow approval processes mean that new flats take years to build. When demand rises faster than supply, prices inevitably climb. A second factor is that property has become a popular investment. Wealthy individuals, some of whom live abroad, buy flats not to live in but to rent out or simply to hold as their value increases. This pushes prices beyond what a young teacher or nurse, earning an ordinary salary, could ever hope to pay.

Several measures could ease the situation. Had governments reformed planning laws earlier, many cities would already have far more affordable homes, so simplifying approvals for medium-sized apartment blocks near public transport should be a priority. Authorities could also build social housing that is rented at a fixed share of tenants' income, as Vienna has done successfully for decades. Finally, higher taxes on homes that are left empty, or on second properties owned purely for profit, would discourage speculation and could fund new construction.

In conclusion, young people are being priced out of cities largely because too few homes are built and too many are bought as investments. If governments increased supply and made speculation less attractive, housing would become noticeably more affordable within a decade.

blocks.x: Many people today prefer to buy imported food rather than local produce. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?

x: In many countries, supermarket shelves are now filled with fruit, cheese and snacks flown in from other continents, and a large number of shoppers choose these over locally grown food. This essay explains why imported products have become so popular and argues that, on balance, the trend is a negative one.

Several factors explain this preference. Imported food is often perceived as higher in quality or safer, particularly in countries where local food safety standards are weakly enforced. Price also matters: large agricultural producers abroad benefit from economies of scale, so their goods can be cheaper than those of small local farmers, even after transport costs. In addition, global advertising and travel have changed tastes, and many middle-class consumers now associate foreign brands with a modern lifestyle.

Although consumers gain more choice, I believe the wider consequences are mostly harmful. The first concern is environmental. Food that is transported thousands of kilometres by air or refrigerated ship generates far higher carbon emissions than produce bought from a nearby market. The second is economic. When shoppers turn away from local produce, small farmers lose income, and rural communities that depend on agriculture may decline as young people leave in search of work. Finally, a heavy reliance on imports makes a country vulnerable: if global supply chains are disrupted, as they were during the pandemic, prices can rise sharply overnight.

In conclusion, people buy imported food mainly because they trust its quality, find it affordable and are drawn to foreign brands. While this gives consumers a wider choice, its environmental and economic costs mean that it is, overall, a negative development.

x: As cities grow, traffic gets worse every year, and governments have to decide where limited transport budgets should go. Some people argue that this money is better spent on buses, trains and trams than on new roads. Some people believe that online learning will eventually replace traditional classrooms in schools and universities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Thesis: Disagree, online learning is a supplement, not a replacement
Body 1: young students need supervision; pandemic experience
Body 2: school teaches social and practical skills; lab, medical training
Body 3 (concession): good for working adults and remote students
Conclusion: classrooms stay at the centre, delivery may change

Since the pandemic, online courses and video lectures have become a normal part of education, and some people now predict that physical classrooms will soon disappear. I disagree. While online learning is a useful addition, I do not believe it can replace schools and universities, mainly because learning depends on people as much as on information.

The first problem is that most students, especially younger ones, need structure and supervision. In a classroom, a teacher can see when a child has stopped listening or has misunderstood a step, and can respond immediately. At home in front of a laptop, the same child can open a game in seconds. When schools closed during the pandemic, many parents discovered how hard it was to keep children focused on lessons through a screen, and the students who were already struggling usually fell furthest behind.

Secondly, school is about more than passing exams. Students learn to work in teams, disagree politely and make friends from different backgrounds, and these skills grow through daily contact rather than through a chat window. Practical subjects make the point even clearer: a chemistry student needs a real laboratory, and a medical student cannot learn to examine patients from a recorded video.

There are, of course, situations where online learning works very well. Adults with full-time jobs can take evening courses that fit their schedules, and students in remote villages can watch lectures from top universities. However, these advantages make online study a valuable supplement, not a replacement.

For these reasons, I think classrooms will remain at the centre of education. Technology will probably change how lessons are delivered, but the supervision, social contact and hands-on practice that schools provide cannot be moved fully online.

Schools prepare children for adult life, but people disagree about which attitude matters more: the drive to compete or the ability to cooperate. Both have value, but in my view cooperation deserves more emphasis, with competition kept in its place as a source of motivation.

Those who favour competition argue that it reflects the real world. Students will later compete for university places, scholarships and jobs, so learning to handle rivalry early may make them more resilient. Competition can also push children to work harder than they otherwise would. A student who knows that the best science project will be shown at a national fair, for instance, is likely to spend extra evenings improving it. From this point of view, removing competition from schools would leave young people unprepared for pressure.

Supporters of cooperation, however, point out that almost every modern job depends on teamwork. Engineers, doctors and software developers rarely succeed alone; they need to share information, divide tasks and settle disagreements. Children who are constantly ranked against their classmates may learn to hide what they know rather than share it. Group projects, by contrast, teach students to listen, to explain ideas clearly and to take responsibility for a shared result.

I find the second argument more convincing. Competition tends to reward only the top few students, while those who regularly come last may lose confidence and stop trying altogether. Cooperation helps every child, including the weakest, because each member of a team has a role to play. Healthy competition can still exist, for example in sports or quizzes, but it should not become the main way schools judge children.
All things considered, competition is useful as a motivator, but learning to work with others is the more valuable lesson for children to carry from school into adult life.

Some people believe that the best way to reduce crime is to give longer prison sentences. Others, however, think there are better alternative ways of reducing crime.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: View A (longer sentences): protects public, deters crime, justice for serious crimes
View B (alternatives): prison creates more criminals, alternatives tackle causes (poverty, addiction, skills)
My opinion: B, but long sentences for dangerous offenders
Example: Norway's rehabilitation system and low reoffending

Governments everywhere want to cut crime, but there is little agreement on how to do it. Some believe that longer prison sentences are the answer, while others argue that money is better spent on prevention and rehabilitation. Although harsh punishment has some role, I believe the second approach is more effective.

People who support longer sentences usually make two points. First, an offender who is in prison cannot harm the public, so keeping dangerous criminals locked up for longer directly protects communities. Second, the threat of a long sentence may discourage people from breaking the law in the first place. For serious violent crimes such as armed robbery or murder, many also feel that a long sentence is simply what justice requires.

Critics, however, argue that prison often makes the problem worse. Inmates, especially young people convicted of minor offences, may spend years alongside experienced criminals and leave with fewer job prospects and stronger criminal contacts. This helps explain why so many former prisoners reoffend. These critics prefer alternatives such as community service, drug treatment and education inside prisons, which deal with the reasons people turn to crime, including poverty, addiction and a lack of skills.

In my opinion, the evidence supports this second view. Norway, for example, focuses on rehabilitation rather than long sentences, and its reoffending rate is among the lowest in Europe. Long sentences should be kept for offenders who pose a real danger to others, but for most crimes, training and treatment protect society better in the long run.
For these reasons, I believe that while prison is necessary for the most dangerous criminals, crime is reduced more effectively by tackling its causes than by simply extending punishment.

Remote work, once rare, has become common in many countries since 2020, particularly in fields such as software, marketing and finance. Although working from home has some real drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater, both for employees and for the companies that employ them.

The most obvious advantage is the time saved on commuting. In a city like Dhaka, an office worker can easily spend two or three hours a day in traffic, and working from home turns that time into extra rest, family time or study. It also cuts spending on transport and meals. Many employees find they concentrate better at home, away from the noise of an open-plan office. For companies, remote teams mean smaller offices and lower rent, and they can hire skilled people who live in other cities or even other countries.

There are, however, genuine disadvantages. Some employees feel isolated without colleagues around them, and the line between work and private life can blur when the laptop never leaves the kitchen table. Junior staff may suffer most, as they miss the informal learning that comes from watching experienced colleagues deal with problems. Besides, not everyone has a quiet room or a reliable internet connection at home.

In my view, these problems are real but manageable. Many firms now use a hybrid model, in which staff come to the office two or three days a week for meetings and training and work from home for the rest. This keeps most of the benefits while reducing isolation and giving new employees time with mentors. The hours lost in commuting, by contrast, can never be recovered.
For these reasons, I believe the advantages of working from home outweigh the disadvantages, particularly when it is combined with regular days in the office.

An increasing number of students are choosing to study at universities in other countries.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of this for the students themselves?

Disadvantages: cost, loneliness/homesickness, recognition at home
Conclusion: summary + 'weigh carefully'

Each year, more young people leave their home countries to study abroad, with the UK, Canada, Australia and Germany among the most popular destinations. This choice can bring students clear academic and personal benefits, but it also involves heavy financial and emotional costs.

The first advantage is access to teaching and facilities that may not be available at home. Many foreign universities have better-equipped laboratories, smaller classes and close links with industry, and a degree from a well-known institution can make a graduate more attractive to employers. Students also improve their English or another foreign language far faster when they use it every day for lectures, shopping and friendship than they would in a classroom at home.

Living abroad also builds independence. A student who must manage a budget, cook, find accommodation and handle official paperwork alone soon becomes more mature and confident. Classmates from many countries widen their view of the world and may become useful contacts later in their careers.

On the other hand, studying abroad is extremely expensive. Even with a partial scholarship, tuition and living costs in cities such as London or Toronto can place a heavy burden on a family, and some students take part-time jobs that leave them too tired to study properly. Loneliness is another serious problem. Far from family and friends, and facing a new climate, food and culture, many international students struggle with homesickness, especially in their first year. Finally, a foreign qualification is not always fully recognised at home, which can make returning difficult.

In short, studying abroad offers a better education, stronger language skills and personal growth, but students need to weigh these gains carefully against the high cost and the strain of living far from home.

The number of overweight children has risen in many countries over the past few decades, and the problem now affects developing nations as well as wealthy ones. The two main causes are changes in diet and a decline in physical activity, and both governments and families can take action to reverse the trend.

The first cause is the food children eat. Fast food, sugary soft drinks and packaged snacks are cheap, available on almost every street corner and heavily advertised on television and social media. Many parents work long hours and have little time to cook, so ready-made meals high in fat and salt have replaced home cooking in many households. The second cause is a lack of exercise. Children who once played outside after school now spend hours on phones, tablets and games consoles, and in crowded cities there are often few safe parks where they could be active.

Several measures could help. Governments could introduce a tax on sugary drinks, as the UK did in 2018, a step that led many manufacturers to cut the sugar content of their products. They could also restrict junk food advertising during children's programmes and require schools to serve healthier lunches. Schools themselves should make physical education a daily activity rather than an occasional lesson.

Families have an equally important part to play. Parents can limit screen time, keep fewer sweets and fizzy drinks at home and encourage children to walk or cycle short distances instead of being driven. Above all, they can set an example, since children tend to copy the eating and exercise habits they see at home.

In short, childhood obesity results mainly from unhealthy food and inactive lifestyles. Tackling it requires both public policy, such as taxes and school programmes, and changes in the daily habits of individual families.

In many developing countries, large numbers of young people are leaving rural areas to live and work in cities.

What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on the countryside?

Write at least 250 words.

Causes (pull): factory and service jobs, colleges, hospitals, electricity
Effects on countryside: loss of young workers, farming harder, services close, cycle of leaving
Positive effect: remittances fund education, housing, small businesses
Example: Bangladesh garment industry around Dhaka and Chattogram

Across much of Asia and Africa, young people are leaving villages for cities in large numbers. This movement is driven mainly by the search for work and better services, and it is having serious effects on the rural communities left behind.

The most important cause is employment. Farm incomes are often low and depend on unpredictable weather, while cities offer jobs in factories, construction and services that pay regular wages. In Bangladesh, for example, the garment industry around Dhaka and Chattogram employs around four million people, many of whom have moved from rural districts. Education is a second reason. Most good colleges and universities are in cities, so ambitious students move there to study and often stay after graduating. Cities also offer better hospitals, a steady electricity supply and faster internet, which make urban life more attractive.

The effects on the countryside are significant. First, villages lose their youngest and most energetic workers, leaving mainly older people and children behind. This makes farming harder, and in some areas land is left unused or rented out. Second, local services decline. When the population falls, schools, shops and clinics may close because they no longer have enough users, which in turn pushes even more families to leave.

Not all the effects are negative, however. Many migrants send part of their wages home, and this money helps their families pay for education, healthcare and better housing. In some villages, these payments have also funded small businesses such as shops or poultry farms.

Taken together, the search for work, education and better services is pulling young people into cities. While the money they send home brings some benefits, rural areas are left with ageing populations and weakening services, which may make the trend even harder to reverse.

Cause paragraph e push (low farm income, weather) ar pull (jobs, colleges, hospitals) duita dik ache, shathe Bangladesh garment industry example.
Effect paragraph e cycle dekhano hoyeche: population falls > services close > more families leave. 'which in turn' eta link kore.
Positive effect (remittances) ek paragraph e, eta essay ke one-sided hote dey na, ar 'effects' plural question ke purnangga answer kore.
Conclusion e notun info nai, kintu ekta shesh insight ache ('harder to reverse'), ja body er cycle theke ashche.

In this essay I will explain why people use social media so much and whether it is positive or negative.
I believe this happens mainly because the platforms are designed to hold attention and because they meet a real need for connection, but that the overall effect of such heavy use is negative.

For many people, checking social media is the first thing they do in the morning and the last thing they do at night. I believe this happens mainly because the platforms are designed to hold attention and because they meet a real need for connection, but that the overall effect of such heavy use is negative.

One reason is the way these apps are built. Feeds on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok never end, and their recommendation systems learn what each user likes and keep showing more of it. Likes, comments and notifications give small rewards that make people want to check again and again. Another reason is social. Friends and relatives now share news, photos and invitations mainly online, so people who stay away may feel left out. For students living far from home, social media is also the easiest way to stay in touch with family.

This trend does have some benefits. Social media helps people keep in contact over long distances, find communities with shared interests and learn from free educational content. Small businesses also use it to reach customers at very little cost.

Nevertheless, I consider the development largely negative. Hours spent scrolling are hours taken away from sleep, exercise, reading and face-to-face conversation. Constant comparison with the carefully edited lives of others can lower self-esteem, particularly among teenagers, and research has linked heavy use with anxiety and poor sleep. False news also spreads quickly on these platforms, as users tend to share dramatic posts before checking whether they are true.

Social media is popular because it is designed to be hard to put down and because it meets a genuine need for contact. However, when it fills most of a person's free time, the harm to health, relationships and access to reliable information outweighs its advantages.

Example: multiplexes in Bangladesh malls vs closing single-screen halls

Streaming services have changed how people watch films, and for many households the sofa has replaced the cinema seat. There are clear practical reasons for this shift, but I do not believe cinemas will disappear, although they are likely to become fewer and more specialised.

The main reasons people watch at home are convenience and cost. A monthly subscription to a service such as Netflix often costs less than cinema tickets for a whole family, and it offers thousands of titles that can be paused, rewatched or viewed on a phone. Home equipment has also improved greatly: large flat-screen televisions and sound bars are now affordable, so the gap in quality between home and cinema is far smaller than it was twenty years ago. In addition, many new films appear on streaming platforms only weeks after their cinema release, so there is little reason to hurry.

Even so, I think cinemas will survive, for two reasons. First, going to the cinema is a social event rather than just a way of seeing a story. Friends and couples go out together, and audiences enjoy laughing or gasping as a group. Second, some films are made for a huge screen. Big releases such as superhero films or space dramas still draw large crowds, and formats like IMAX offer an experience that no living room can copy.

What is more likely is that the industry will change shape. Smaller cinemas showing ordinary films may close, while the survivors offer premium seats, food and special events to justify higher prices. In Bangladesh, for instance, multiplex cinemas in shopping malls have expanded even as many older single-screen halls have shut down.

In short, people watch films at home because it is cheaper, easier and increasingly high in quality. Cinemas will lose some customers, but as places for shared experiences and spectacular films, they are unlikely to vanish completely.

x: Thesis: Largely agree, especially for unhealthy products; full ban hard to enforce
Body 1: children cannot judge adverts
Body 2: pressure on families; junk food and obesity
Body 3 (concession): online ads hard to control; practical partial ban

Children today see thousands of advertisements a year on television, YouTube and mobile games. Some people believe that all advertising directed at children should be banned. I agree with this view to a large extent, particularly for products that can harm their health, although a complete ban would be difficult to enforce.

The main argument for a ban is that young children cannot judge advertisements critically. Many children under about eight cannot reliably tell the difference between an advert and an ordinary programme, and even older children rarely understand that an advert is designed to persuade them. When cartoon characters promote sugary cereals or expensive toys, children simply believe what they see. It seems unfair for companies with large marketing budgets to target an audience that cannot defend itself.

Advertising aimed at children also creates problems for families. Children who want the latest toy or snack often put pressure on their parents, and this can cause arguments at home and push low-income families to spend money they cannot afford. Adverts for junk food are especially harmful, since they encourage eating habits that contribute to childhood obesity.

However, banning every advert would not be simple. Children now spend much of their time online, where advertising is mixed with entertainment through influencers and sponsored videos, which are hard to regulate. Some adverts, such as those for books or road safety campaigns, may even be useful. A more practical approach might be strict bans on unhealthy food advertising and on adverts during children's programmes, together with clear labelling of sponsored content.

For these reasons, I largely support restricting advertising aimed at children, as they are easily influenced and the effects on health and family budgets can be serious. Governments should start with the most harmful products and extend the rules to online platforms over time.
notes: 'To a large extent' + 'particularly for...' + 'although...' : ek sentence e position, focus ar limit tin tai clear.
Body 1 er main idea (children cannot judge adverts) ke age-specific detail (under about eight) diye support kora.
Body 2 effect chain: adverts > pressure on parents > arguments, overspending; junk food ads > obesity.
Concession paragraph e practical solution ('strict bans on unhealthy food advertising') ache, ja 'largely agree' position ke logical kore.

Some people think that international tourism damages local cultures, while others believe it helps to protect them. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: View A: customs changed for visitors; residents pushed out (Venice)
View B: money for heritage and crafts (Paharpur)
My view: B, if tourism is managed

Mass tourism brings millions of visitors to historic towns and traditional communities every year. Some argue that this contact slowly destroys local culture, while others believe tourist money helps to keep traditions alive. In my opinion, tourism can do both, but when it is sensibly managed, its protective effect is stronger.

Those who see tourism as harmful point out that local customs are often changed to suit visitors. Traditional dances may be cut into short performances for hotel guests, and handmade crafts may be replaced by cheap souvenirs made in factories. In popular destinations such as Venice, rising rents and crowds have pushed many residents out of the historic centre, so the places tourists come to see gradually lose the people who gave them their character.

Supporters of tourism, on the other hand, argue that it gives communities a financial reason to protect their heritage. Entrance fees help to pay for the repair of temples, palaces and museums, and visitors who buy local crafts allow artisans to keep practising skills that might otherwise disappear. In Bangladesh, for example, visitors to the ancient Buddhist monastery at Paharpur bring income to nearby villages and draw attention to the need to preserve the site.

I find the second view more convincing, provided tourism is properly controlled. Limits on visitor numbers, rules on building near heritage sites and support for genuine local businesses can reduce the damage while keeping the income. Without tourism, many small communities would have neither the money nor the motivation to protect their traditions.

To my mind, tourism is not in itself a threat to local culture. When it is well managed, it gives people both the means and the reason to preserve the customs and places that make their communities distinctive.
notes: Intro te mixed opinion, kintu clear direction: 'its protective effect is stronger', shathe condition 'when it is sensibly managed'.

pages.h: Practice 23: model essay (problem and solution, technology and work)

blocks.x:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to do jobs that were previously done by people. What problems might this cause, and what can be done to reduce them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

x: Problems: job loss, inequality, bias and unclear responsibility
Solutions: retraining, taxes or training budgets from companies, human review of AI decisions
Matching: each solution answers one problem

Artificial intelligence can now write reports, answer customer questions and even help doctors read X-rays. As these systems take over tasks once done by people, several problems are likely to appear, but governments, companies and workers can take steps to reduce them.

The most obvious problem is job loss. Workers in call centres, data entry and basic translation face the greatest risk, because their tasks follow clear patterns that software can copy. Many of these employees cannot easily move into new careers, especially if they are older or have limited education. A second problem is inequality. The profits from automation tend to go to the companies that own the technology and the small number of highly skilled people who build it, while wages for routine work may fall.

There are also concerns about fairness and responsibility. AI systems learn from past data, so they can repeat existing biases, for example by rejecting job applicants from certain backgrounds. When such a system makes a mistake, it is often unclear who should be held responsible: the company, the developer or the user.

Several measures could reduce these problems. Governments could fund retraining programmes so that workers whose jobs are automated can learn new skills, such as checking the output of AI tools, or move into fields like nursing where human contact still matters. Companies that save money through automation could be required to contribute through taxes or training budgets. Finally, laws should require important AI decisions, such as those about hiring or loans, to be explained and reviewed by a human.

In short, the spread of AI at work may lead to job losses, wider inequality and unfair decisions. Retraining, a fairer sharing of the gains and clear rules on responsibility can reduce these risks, so that the technology benefits society as a whole.
notes: Intro te concrete examples (reports, customer questions, X-rays) diye topic real kora, tarpor task er duita part preview.
Problem paragraph e 'because' diye keno oi jobs risk e ta explain kora: 'tasks follow clear patterns'.
Problems ar solutions matched: job loss > retraining; inequality > taxes/training budgets; bias and responsibility > human review law.
Modal verbs precise: 'could fund', 'could be required', 'should require'. Possibility ar recommendation alada.
Hedging: 'are likely to appear', 'may fall', 'tend to go'. Future technology niye careful, realistic tone.
